10 Years Of Using Linux: How It Was Before, And How It Became

Linux was never able to entice me to try it… WINDOWS did what Linux never could… it DROVE me to Linux.

It first threatened to do so with Windows Vista… I tried kubuntu at the time but found the Linux experience very schizophrenic at the time. Parts of it were so smooth and refined, but other parts were course and lacking features that I considered hyper-basic. (I distinctly remember spending 3 hours learning an entire language of driver-settings-semantics and editing half a dozen hidden system files just to turn of tap-to-click on my touch pad mouse).

Ultimately Windows came out with 7, and 3rd parties came out with hacks for Windows more annoying ~~bugs~~, er I mean "features". So I abandoned the Linux world for a newly tamed Windows. But then 8.x came out and it became clear that MS was going further in a direction away from users like me. 7 was still working, so I resolved to skip 8.x and hope for a return to sanity from MS with the next version.

Then Windows 10 happened. Win10 was different from all of the abomination "features" that MS had tried to foist upon us before. Before, it was just a matter of figuring how to bypass/disable/opt-out of the new feature. With the Windows as a service model however, and its integrated a-volitional updates and telemetry, it was clear that MS was abandoning the OS as a stand-alone machine model, but rather treating it as a managed device on a network service. THAT MODEL CAN'T BE BYPASSED OR REDEEMED. It was a declaration of war against users like me.

Now I HAD to switch to Linux... It literally is the only remaining desktop OS that embraces the desktop machine as both under the User's control, and as a stand alone device. In the intervening years, Linux had massively matured. Better distros like LinuxMint with xfce are a large part of that. When I had flirted with it before, one could hardly go 1 hour of using it without going out to the command line or editing config files. Now, it is quite possible to only need to do that sort of thing once or twice per install. I still need VMs to run some legacy software, and the Linux world is notably lacking in advanced filemanagers. Also, contrary to the article's contention LibreOffice still does not play well enough with MS Office.

Keep an eye on Haiku OS... right now its still a very very good beta test but as the culture wars hit Linux and the corporations buy control of the linux foundation expect Linux have problems in the future.
